Lessons.Title: Which Variable to Solve for? (Part 2)
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning objective: isolate a target variable from multi-variable constraints before entering data, and use the resulting expression to evaluate multiple scenarios efficiently. Original Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 2 Lesson 9, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/2/9/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). Addressing HSA-CED.A.3, HSA-CED.A.4 and HSA-REI.B.3.

Original independent cargo model: a freight vessel has at most 150 tonnes available. Let c≥0 be whole-number containers of 2.5 tonnes and t≥0 be whole-number crates of 3.75 tonnes. Constraint 2.5c+3.75t≤150. At capacity equality, solve for c=(150−3.75t)/2.5=60−1.5t. Because c,t are integers, not every point on this continuous line represents a valid loading plan.

Evaluate with t=12: c=60−18=42 containers and cargo mass 2.5×42+3.75×12=105+45=150 tonnes. With t=13, c=40.5 from equality is not a possible whole number of containers; at most floor(40.5)=40 fit without exceeding capacity. A spreadsheet can recalculate this but an authored numerical table is not proof of actual software interaction.

Student task: rearrange the equation in two ways (solve c in terms of t, t in terms of c), build a labelled table, test boundaries including negative and non-integer outputs, and critique a partner's feasible cargo plan. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, 8 maximum): correct transformation, valid domain, correct boundary and rounding, and explanation of technology simulation versus observed tool use.

KeyConcepts.Title: Solve before substitution
KeyConcepts.Definition: An isolated variable expression can be reused for many input scenarios.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Keep numerator and denominator grouped with parentheses.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equality and capacity
KeyConcepts.Definition: Equality is the full-load boundary; inequality allows lighter feasible loads.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not confuse equal load with all feasible shipments.

KeyConcepts.Title: Integer domain
KeyConcepts.Definition: Physical item counts are nonnegative integers.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Take floor for maximum count if a continuous value is fractional.
KeyConcepts.Example: For t=13, maximum c is 40, not 40.5.

WorkedExamples.Title: Isolate containers
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve 2.5c+3.75t=150 for c.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use equivalence-preserving algebra, show domain restrictions and independently check a test value.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check fractional capacity boundary
WorkedExamples.Question: What is the maximum integer c if t=13 crates?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use equivalence-preserving algebra, show domain restrictions and independently check a test value.
Steps: A physical count must be whole and nonnegative, so maximum c=40.

WorkedExamples.Title: Rearrange for crates
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve full-load equation for t and evaluate c=30.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use equivalence-preserving algebra, show domain restrictions and independently check a test value.
WorkedExamples.Check: All counts are nonnegative integers and mass equals capacity.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating every real graph point as an admissible load
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Only nonnegative integer combinations describe actual objects.

SummaryPoints: An isolated variable expression simplifies repeated modeling calculations.
Cargo capacity is an inequality with an equality boundary.
For t=13, no more than 40 whole containers of 2.5 tonnes can fit.
Teacher reviews feasibility, unit interpretation and truthful technology evidence.

Visuals.Title: Original mathematically checkable table
Visuals.Description: Independent first-party numerical model; each row has an exact textual interpretation.
